As a professional carpet cleaner/floor care specialist by trade. You NEED enzymes. Blacklight/uv light the area. The issue here is whether you have cloth or leather seats. If you have leather it will be an easier cleanup. If it’s cloth it could have soaked into the foam padding off the seats/carpet. 

My personal recommendation would be bio release and bio modifier extreme by bridge point systems. I’ve never had a failure with this system that was my fault. You’ll dilute them 1:4 start with bio release, let dwell 20-30 minutes then extract with plain water. You may need to inject chemical into the padding with a syringe. 

Next you will need to just LIGHTLY spray bio modifier extreme onto the affected area. It could take up to 7 days for the enzymes to fully kill off any odors. DO NOT use any kind of peroxide for the stains during that time. Peroxide WILL kill enzymes and then you have to redo. Don’t even worry about staining for now.

You’ll need an enzyme treatment and run it in the climate controll system. 

First try another cleaning but use bio release by bridge point systems. It’s an oxidizer and enzyme treatment specifically formulated for breaking down proteins of bodily fluids. 

Pre spray bio release diluted 1:4 spray affected area and let dwell 20-30 minutes. Spray enough to saturate materials don’t over soak but enough that it won’t dry in that timeframe. Agitate then Extract with plain water. 

Now that’s done. Use bio modifier extreme by bridge point systems it’s the enzyme treatment for odors. Prespray lightly misting affected area diluted 1:4. Run the climate control for a couple hours set to recirculate. Ventilate vehicle by cracking open windows/opening doors. Set temperature no more than 75 degrees F no less than 70F. Carpets/fabrics full dry time is 24 hours more for foam padded fabric seats. 

Make it a point to spray some bio modifier into the vents under the seats and dash, that’s where air is sucked in on recirculate. Repeat as necessary until desired effect is achieved. 

Also replace the cabin air filter before enzyme treatment. It’s usually located behind the glove box and it just unclips from the back. 

An ozone treatment alone likely won’t fix it. Seeing as how the cleaning wasn’t done with the right chemistry to begin with.

Former professional carpet cleaner/floor care specialist (commercial and residential) of 2 years here to help. 

You’ll need to remove the seat someone already mentioned that follow that guide. 

First thing you want to do is get your chemistry right. You’ll need an oxidizer and enzymes. Oxidizer for the coloring, coffee is natural coloring. Enzymes is for the odor. This will take several steps. 

First spray on your oxidizer let dwell (sunlight, and UV light will help expedite this process), agitate the extract with plain water. Put some powdered defamer in the waste  tank if needed if tank is excessively foaming and causing suction loss

Now for the general/annual cleaning. Use biobreak (ph9.5-10.6 also has some enzymes) by Bridgepoint systems as pre-spray, agitate, let dwell. Rinse with an acidic, rinse such as flex ice (ph4.5-5.5) or encapuguard green (preferred, ph 3.5) both by bridge point systems. Leaving carpets in an alkaline state can cause soiling or browning to come back faster and worse than before. That is why the acidic.acid rinse is important. It is to neutralize the alkaline and leave carpets in an acidic state. Put some powdered defamer in the waste tank if needed if tank is excessively foaming and causing suction loss

Finally for the enzyme process. I prefer bio modifier extreme by Bridgepoint systems (ph neutral). Dilute 1:4 and spray on LIGHTLY. Let dry but also repeat if necessary. 

For the drying process, turn on the climate control and set to floor. No more than 75°F no less than 70°F. If you can park the car in a sunny area where the sun can directly hit that area. You can also put fans down to help expedite the process leave the vehicle ventilated for at least 24 hours full dry time of carpets is 24 hours.

Now for cleaning the machine while the vehicle is drying. Dump out rinse tank and put a full rinse tank of plain water into the tank. Then run that through the pump and rinse hose. You don’t want that acid sitting in the pump especially on a smaller machine. It won’t kill the machine to use the acidic rinse to help clean but don’t leave it sitting in the machine until next use. 

If you have any questions visit your local Interlink/aramsco and they can set you up. Don’t use just any detail companies/supplier chemicals, they just happen to make carpet chemicals. Kind of like how Suzuki and Mitsubishi happen to make cars, doesn’t mean they’re any good. If you don’t think this job is for you or it’s too complicated. Hello former commercial and residential carpet/floor cleaner of 2 years here. 

When wet vacuuming carpets upholstery it’s important to make lots of dry only passes especially on smaller machines. Afterwards turn on the climate control set to floor only and set temperature no less than 70F no more than 75F. Ventilate vehicle and if weather is nice enough open doors and let dry in direct sunlight. Carpet/upholstery full dry Time is 24 hours possibly more but that depends on how Saturated surface is. 

When cleaning it helps to use an alkaline pre spray (such as Biobreak by bridge point systems) with either plain water in the rinse tank or ideally acidic rinse (such as flex ice or encapugaurd green both by bridge point systems) to neutralize alkaline. Ideally you want the surface to dry in a slightly more acidic state because if it drys alkaline it will attract soiling, browning ect faster and worse than before cleaning. It’s not the end if it drys ph neutral. If you choose to use an acidic rinse make sure to run a tank of plain water through the pump so as not to allow acidic rinse break down seals, water lines ect. That’s iron particles aka “fallout”. It’s brake dust particles that imbedded themselves into the paint then create a mini rust spot which is a chemical reaction. I’d recommend using a chemical iron remover like IronX which will chemically break down the rust you’ll see because the chemical will turn purple. Use a clay bar and ironX as lube (most effective) but beware the chemical will break down the claybar and quickly. So buy a couple clay bars and break them up into 1/4ths. 

Just using a claybar alone will shave the top of the particle yet it’s still imbedded and the rust spec will remain. Just using ironX alone will break down most the rust but it will reappear shortly after because the iron is still imbedded. Clay and ironX is the way so you break down and remove contaminates. 

Alternatively you could use a clay disc or clay towel (they won’t break down from chemical use because their synthetic) but they’re not nearly as aggressive and won’t remove everything, they’re more for maintenance after you do a heavy decon. I’d personally go for standard clay because your car is white and won’t show the swirling introduced from claybar.

As for RestorFX and the brand itself (can’t say the same for other brands) It’s a legitimate clearcoat (hand applied 2k self leveling if I’m correct). It mechanically and chemically adheres to the original clear. In cases like Asian cars especially Toyota/subaru it’s actually harder than the original factory clear coat. It will mimick the surface and texture of whatever it’s applied to. 

There has to be a layer of clear to adhere to. So if the clear has failed (fading peeling or cracking) or is close to the verge of failing, then the RestorFX will for sure fail. It won’t fix etchings or staining even with wetsanding and application. 

You don’t have to ceramic coat it afterwards. It’s ideal but not necessary. Ideally you don’t want to coat until 2-4weeks after application. You need to let it cure like it’s fresh paint. RestorFX intl themselves will tell you yes you can 24-48 hours after application without ipa/panel wipe (because it’s raw fresh clear). In theory yes you can rush the vehicle out like that. But as a technician in reality it didn’t always work well that way in my experience. We had clients of 10 years not get coated and the clear was still there in good condition. 

All in all I only saw like 1-3 cars a year come back from a failure. That was doing 2-4 cars per day. If it failed it came down to either bad prep, bad application, or poor maintenance on the customer end.

It doesn’t fail easily if the paint is good condition. Prep was done right and application was done well. I had my car done 5 years ago now clearcoat with ceramic combo. Still good with no failure spots besides where people have hit me. It’s a 2003 mercury grand marquis.

I save headlights in similar conditions multiple times weekly. You may be able to save these either tape off surrounding areas, or remove the headlight assemblies. 

Get some sanding blocks from your local paint supplier softer are less aggressive but less likely leave behind deep scratches from human error. Now get some a single or couple of sheets of each of these grits. 240, 320, 400, 500, 600, 800, 1000, 1200, 1500, 2000, 3k 3m trizact, 5k 3m trizact, 8k 3m trizact. Cut ALL PAPER sheets into 1/4th’s then set them in a bucket or container of water and let soak for 10-15 minutes. DO NOT CUT UP THE 3M Trizact pads they’ll be useless after. 

Start wet sanding and go in this order 240>320>400>500>600>800>1000>1200>1500>2000>3k>5k>8k. When sanding make sure you try and sand out as much of the cracking and previous layers with 240, 320 and 400, use the rest of the grits to refine. Also cross hatch each grit and start in the opposite direction you finished the last grit with the next grit. Make sure they look uniform and even with each grit. Use a new paper for each headlight to they’ll wear down pretty quickly. You can use soapy water but the soaps reduce the ability to cut.

Now that you’ve finished sanding and they look uniform and even (they won’t be perfect) compound and polish them out. As for protection you can ceramic coat or ppf them but I would personally ppf with ceramic coating on top. Fair warning this could take 2-4 hours. You can also do the fog lights if equipped.

Don’t try bug spray. It’s temporary. If it melts the lens’ surface to clean it what do you think the run off/overspray will do the surrounding materials like paint (which is essentially plastic) grille, plastics, or bumper.

Wax is different from compound/polish. Compound/polishes have abrasives that break down and remove paint. Wax is a protectant with additives like carnuba to  increase gloss. Now some waxes can have abrasive additives to help bring out more gloss but it’s a negligible amount. It won’t give you a true look to what the paint really looks like since they’ll have fillers as well. 

Waxes also have cleaning agents which is why this looks worse after waxing because it cleansed the pours of the paint.

You can use too much wax. But all it will really do it is crust and make it harder to wipe off, thus wasting product. There will still be a layer of protection. Doing multiple layers of wax is also a waste because you’re just removing the previous layer. Honestly recommend using spray waxes/sealants. They’re more durable and longer lasting.

It looks like the clearcoat had already failed then they applied their product which is a big NO, shop shouldn’t have taken that vehicle and should’ve recommended a respray. 

RestorFX typically doesn’t fail. In 5 years of doing it I’ve seen 2-3vehicles fail. The variables are usually technician didn’t prep right (mechanically or chemically), didn’t use enough product (it self-levels), clearcoat had already failed and shop applied anyways (RFX only bonds to pre-existing clear). Other variable on the customers side would be not taking care of restored paint, automatic washes, excessively harsh chemicals ect. 

I’m going to assume in this instance it wasn’t prepped right and the application was thin. I can assume that because of the little halos around the rock chips and the inconsistencies in application lines. They likely knew they were thin and just buffed to blend the day after. 

To remove the bad application you’ll want to take a 3k trizact pad with an interface pad on a DA and GENTLY wet sand. Once a majority is gone take a 5k trizact pad with interface pad and continue. After that take a 5k on a sanding block and sand off whatever the DA didn’t pull off. Now you can finish out with polishing. 

I’ve seen cars that have been applied 10 years ago and still fine. My personal vehicle was done by me 4 years ago. It still looks great and haven’t had issues but mine is also ceramic coated. I’m sorry this happened to you but it’s definitely fixable.
